```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(nnet)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
```

## Why this matters

Neural networks arrive with more mystique than any other method in this course, and the
mystique gets in the way twice. It makes people reach for one when a linear model would
do, and it makes people who could easily understand the mechanics assume they cannot.

The mechanics are unremarkable. A neuron is a weighted sum of its inputs passed through
one fixed function. A layer is several neurons reading the same inputs. A network is a
couple of layers stacked. Everything that makes deep learning hard in practice —
training, tuning, the compute — sits on top of that, and none of it changes what the
object is.

This page builds one up from a regression you have already fitted.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea: one neuron is a regression

A **neuron** takes the inputs $x_1, \dots, x_p$, multiplies each by a **weight**, adds a
constant called the **bias**, and passes the total through an **activation function** $g$:

$$h = g(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_p x_p + b)$$

Read that without the word "neuron" and it is a generalised linear model: the weights are
regression coefficients, the bias is the intercept, and the activation is the inverse link
function. If $g$ is the identity, you have linear regression. If $g$ is the logistic
function, you have logistic regression.

That is not an analogy. It is the same arithmetic, and we can check it.

```{r}
#| label: one-neuron-linear
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

d <- survey |>
  transmute(y     = log1p(abundance),
            depth = as.numeric(scale(depth_m)),
            temp  = as.numeric(scale(temperature_c)),
            chl   = as.numeric(scale(log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3)))) |>
  drop_na()

linear <- lm(y ~ depth + temp + chl, data = d)

set.seed(1)
one_neuron <- nnet(y ~ depth + temp + chl, data = d,
                   size = 0, skip = TRUE, linout = TRUE,
                   maxit = 2000, trace = FALSE)

tibble(term = names(coef(linear)),
       `lm()` = round(coef(linear), 4),
       `one neuron` = round(as.numeric(coef(one_neuron)), 4))
```

`size = 0, skip = TRUE` asks `nnet` for a network with no hidden layer — inputs wired
straight to the output — and `linout = TRUE` makes the output activation the identity. The
two fits agree to eight decimal places. Swap `linout` for `entropy = TRUE` and the same
call reproduces `glm(family = binomial)` to four.

So a neuron on its own buys you nothing. The interesting question is what a *layer* of
them buys.

## What a hidden layer adds

A **hidden layer** is a set of neurons that read the inputs and whose outputs are read by
the next layer rather than by you. They are hidden in the sense that nothing outside the
model ever sees their values.

![A network with three inputs, one hidden layer of four units and one output. Every arrow
carries a weight; every circle in the hidden and output layers also has a bias. The
highlighted arrow is $w_{21}$, the weight from temperature into the first hidden
unit.](img/network-schematic.svg){#fig-schematic fig-alt="A diagram in three columns. On
the left, three circles labelled depth, temp and chl. In the middle, four circles labelled
h1 to h4. On the right, a single circle labelled y-hat. Arrows run from every input circle
to every hidden circle, and from every hidden circle to the output circle. One arrow, from
temp to h1, is drawn in blue and labelled w21. A note below reads: each hidden unit
computes h equals g of w1 times depth plus w2 times temp plus w3 times chl plus b."}

Here is the part that matters, and it is worth stating bluntly because it is usually
buried. **If the activation function $g$ is linear, the whole network is linear.** A
weighted sum of weighted sums is a weighted sum; stacking a hundred layers of them gets
you a straight line with a hundred times as many parameters. The nonlinearity of $g$ is
not a detail of implementation. It is the only reason a network can do anything a linear
model cannot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-activations
#| fig-cap: "Four activation functions. The identity is what makes a network collapse to a linear model. The other three bend, each in its own way, and that bend is the entire source of a network's flexibility."
#| fig-alt: "Four small line plots side by side over an input range of minus four to four. Identity is a straight diagonal line. Logistic is an S-curve rising from zero to one, centred at zero. Tanh is a similar S-curve rising from minus one to one. ReLU is flat at zero for negative inputs then rises as a straight diagonal for positive ones, giving a sharp corner at the origin."
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
grid_z <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)

tibble(z = rep(grid_z, 4),
       value = c(grid_z, plogis(grid_z), tanh(grid_z), pmax(grid_z, 0)),
       activation = rep(c("identity", "logistic", "tanh", "ReLU"), each = length(grid_z))) |>
  mutate(activation = fct_inorder(activation)) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#c9d1d7", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ activation, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "weighted sum entering the unit", y = NULL)
```

The logistic and tanh curves are S-shaped: flat, then rising, then flat again. ReLU
(*rectified linear unit*) is flat below zero and a straight line above it. All three are
just bends — none of them is doing anything clever on its own.

## Worked example: two bends make a hump

Abundance in this survey peaks at an intermediate temperature and falls away either side.
A straight line cannot represent a hump. Let us see how much hidden layer it takes.

```{r}
#| label: temp-sweep
temp_data <- survey |>
  transmute(y = log1p(abundance), temp = as.numeric(scale(temperature_c))) |>
  drop_na()

fit_units <- function(h) {
  set.seed(9)
  if (h == 0) {
    nnet(y ~ temp, data = temp_data, size = 0, skip = TRUE, linout = TRUE,
         maxit = 2000, trace = FALSE)
  } else {
    nnet(y ~ temp, data = temp_data, size = h, linout = TRUE, decay = 1e-4,
         maxit = 2000, trace = FALSE)
  }
}

sweep <- map_dfr(c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10), \(h) {
  f <- fit_units(h)
  tibble(`hidden units` = h,
         weights = length(coef(f)),
         `training RMSE` = round(sqrt(mean((temp_data$y - as.numeric(predict(f, temp_data)))^2)), 4))
})
sweep
```

Nothing happens until the second hidden unit, and then everything happens at once. Zero
units is a straight line, RMSE 0.877 — and note in @fig-hump that the best straight line
through a hump *rises*, because the cold tail of this survey is lower than the warm one.
A linear fit here does not just miss the optimum, it reports the wrong sign. One unit is a
single S-curve — still monotone, still unable to come back down — and it improves the fit
by 0.016. Two units drop the RMSE to 0.776, and units three, five and ten add essentially
nothing after that.

Two is the magic number because **two opposing S-curves subtract to make a bump**. One
unit switches on as temperature rises; the second switches on a little later with a
negative weight into the output, pulling the curve back down. That is the whole mechanism,
and it generalises: a hidden layer builds arbitrary shapes by adding and subtracting
shifted copies of one bend.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hump
#| fig-cap: "Fitted temperature response with zero, one, two and five hidden units, over the binned station means. A straight line cannot turn over; one S-curve cannot come back down; two can. The true optimum in the simulation is 9 °C."
#| fig-alt: "A scatter of pale binned mean points forming a hump: about 0.29 at three and a half degrees, rising to a peak of about 1.63 near eight and a half degrees, then falling to about 0.66 at fourteen and a half. Four fitted lines are overlaid. The zero-unit line is straight and rises gently from about 1.03 on the left to about 1.39 on the right, passing through the hump without following it. The one-unit line is nearly flat at about 1.27 across most of the range, then bends down after about eleven degrees to about 0.52 at the right edge. The two-unit and five-unit lines lie almost on top of each other: both climb steeply from near zero at the left edge to a peak of about 1.67 just below nine degrees, then fall away to about 0.4 at the right."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
temp_mean <- mean(survey$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE)
temp_sd   <- sd(survey$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE)

grid <- tibble(temp = seq(min(temp_data$temp), max(temp_data$temp), length.out = 300))

curves <- map_dfr(c(0, 1, 2, 5), \(h) {
  grid |> mutate(y = as.numeric(predict(fit_units(h), grid)),
                 `hidden units` = factor(h))
}) |>
  mutate(temperature_c = temp * temp_sd + temp_mean)

binned <- survey |>
  drop_na(temperature_c) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(temperature_c, breaks = seq(2, 18, by = 1))) |>
  summarise(temperature_c = mean(temperature_c), y = mean(log1p(abundance)),
            n = n(), .by = bin) |>
  filter(n >= 10)

ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, y)) +
  geom_point(data = binned, colour = "#9aa5ad", size = 2.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 9, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c9d1d7") +
  geom_line(aes(colour = `hidden units`), linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.25, y = 0.25, label = "true optimum", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2, colour = "#77818a") +
  labs(x = "temperature (°C)", y = "mean log1p(abundance)", colour = "hidden units")
```

## What the results mean

Two hidden units, seven weights, and the curve lands its peak at 8.7 °C against a true
optimum of 9.0 °C — recovered from the data with no one telling the model that the
relationship was humped.

That is the real selling point of a network, and it is worth being precise about it. A
polynomial term or a spline would have found the same hump, faster and with a standard
error attached. What the network did *not* need was for you to know in advance which
variable to bend and how. On one predictor that is a small convenience. On forty, where
the shape might be an interaction between three of them, it stops being small.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths, if you want it
With $H$ hidden units, weights $W \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times H}$, hidden biases
$b \in \mathbb{R}^{H}$, output weights $v \in \mathbb{R}^{H}$ and output bias $c$, the
network computes

$$\hat y = v^{\top} g(W^{\top} x + b) + c$$

where $g$ is applied elementwise. If $g$ is the identity this is
$\hat y = (Wv)^{\top} x + (v^{\top}b + c)$ — a linear model with coefficients $Wv$, no
matter how large $H$ is.
:::

## How many parameters is that?

Every arrow in @fig-schematic is a number to be estimated, and the count grows faster than
people expect. For $p$ inputs, one hidden layer of $H$ units and one output:

$$\text{weights} = \underbrace{(p + 1)H}_{\text{into the hidden layer}} + \underbrace{H + 1}_{\text{out of it}}$$

```{r}
#| label: parameter-count
tibble(`hidden units` = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32)) |>
  mutate(`weights (12 inputs)` = 13 * `hidden units` + `hidden units` + 1,
         `rows per weight, n = 720` = round(720 / `weights (12 inputs)`, 1))
```

The survey has 12 predictor columns once `substrate` and `season` are dummy-coded. At 16
hidden units that is 225 weights for 720 stations — three rows per parameter. A linear
model on the same columns fits 13. There is no rule that says three rows per parameter is
too few, but you should know the number before you fit, not after the result looks odd.

## Where this breaks down

**The weights do not mean anything individually.** In a linear model, the coefficient on
depth is the effect of depth. In a network, depth's contribution is spread across $H$
weights that interact through the activations, and two networks fitted to the same data
reach different weights with the same predictions. There is nothing to report. §10 covers
[what you can extract instead](../10-interpretation/feature-importance.qmd).

**Nothing is stopping the flexibility.** The hump on this page was fitted with
`decay = 1e-4`, a regularisation penalty, precisely because an unpenalised ten-unit
network will happily fit the noise between the station bins. Everything §5 said about
[model complexity](../05-generalisation/model-complexity.qmd) applies with more force here,
not less.

**It is a model of the inputs you gave it.** A network reads a table of numbers. It has no
idea that two of your columns are longitude and latitude, or that your rows are a time
series. The architectures that exploit that structure — convolutional, recurrent — are
about *wiring*, not about neurons, and they are outside this course.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- A single neuron with an identity activation **is** linear regression; with a logistic
  activation it **is** logistic regression. We reproduced both to four decimal places or better.
- A **hidden layer** is several neurons reading the same inputs. Their values are never
  reported and have no units.
- **The activation function is the whole trick.** With a linear activation, any number of
  layers collapses to one linear model.
- Two hidden units — seven weights — were enough to recover a humped temperature response
  with its peak at 8.7 °C against a true 9.0 °C. One was not enough, and five added
  nothing.
- Count your parameters before you fit. Sixteen hidden units on this survey is 225 weights
  for 720 rows.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Refit the temperature sweep with `decay = 0`. How much does the ten-unit training RMSE
   improve, and what happens to the shape of the fitted curve between the binned points?
2. Replace `log1p(abundance)` with the binary `present` column and `linout = TRUE` with
   `entropy = TRUE`. Does two hidden units still capture the temperature optimum?
